facts.text: Accident evidence emphasizes different travel directions: 67% of 22 cases involving all surface equipment in 2000–2006 involved reversing, whereas 12 of 13 haul-truck cases in 2005–2021 involved forward travel; British cross-industry data also highlight reversing. These findings reflect population differences in machine type, site type and country rather than a contradiction, because warehouses, waste yards, construction sites, roadworks and mine haul roads have different traffic geometries and machine mixes.
facts.quote: 67% reversing (2000 to 2006, all surface equipment, 22 cases) [2] against 12 of 13 forward (2005 to 2021, haul trucks only) [4], and British cross-industry data that highlight reversing [5].

facts.text: Workers report jarring and jolting from stops, whereas MSHA is unaware of any such injuries. The disagreement over operator injury from stops remains unresolved, and no measurement exists.
facts.quote: Worker reports of jarring and jolting [11] against MSHA being unaware of any such injuries [22]. Unresolved; no measurement exists.

facts.text: An unnamed manufacturer reported a 5–10% production loss to MSHA, whereas two operators reported recovery to baseline productivity. These productivity claims remain unresolved stakeholder claims.
facts.quote: A 5 to 10% production loss reported to MSHA by an unnamed manufacturer against two operators' reports of recovery to baseline [22]. Unresolved stakeholder claims.

facts.text: A highly sensitive sensor minimizes missed detections but produces the nuisance burden observed in the field, whereas South African and Australian guidance stress context-aware discrimination. Neither always alarming when close nor aggressive alarm suppression is supported across all tasks.
facts.quote: A highly sensitive sensor minimizes missed detections but produces the nuisance burden seen in the field [3]; South African and Australian guidance stress context-aware discrimination [20, 14].

facts.text: In the immediate-stop versus controlled-deceleration debate, earlier intervention avoids contact, whereas abrupt stops reduce acceptance and may add risk. ISO allows speed reduction, stopping or motion inhibition rather than prescribing one response.
facts.quote: Earlier intervention avoids contact, but abrupt stops reduce acceptance and may add risk; ISO allows speed reduction, stopping or motion inhibition rather than prescribing one [12, 81].

facts.text: The cry-wolf effect is strong in some on-road truck Forward Collision Warning data but absent in air traffic control and some driving-simulator studies. All of this evidence is non-mining evidence.
facts.quote: Strong in some on-road truck FCW data [16], absent in air traffic control and some driving-simulator studies [75, 18]. All of this is non-mining evidence.

facts.text: NSW and NIOSH bowtie work favor lower-level controls—EMESRT Levels 1–6, including site design, segregation and procedures—with collision systems at Levels 7–9 as backup, whereas South Africa mandates Level 9 intervention by law. South Africa's Mine Health and Safety Act regulation 8.10.1.2(b) was gazetted on 21 December 2022.
facts.quote: South Africa mandates Level 9 intervention by law (Mine Health and Safety Act regulation 8.10.1.2(b), gazetted 21 December 2022) [90, 91, 54]. **Independent** and **Expert opinion**.

entities.name: Mine Health and Safety Act regulation 8.10.1.2(b)
